0b13e128d1:
This chapter is about two things. First, how to cut a large task into pieces a model can do well. Second, how to keep, resume, branch and abandon the conversation that the work lives in.

The first half covers fixed pipelines (prompt chaining), per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass, and adaptive plans that grow from findings.

The second half covers what a session actually is, and what --resume and fork_session do on the wire and on disk. It covers what resuming costs, and why a resumed agent believes tool results that are no longer true. And it covers when to start fresh with a summary instead. Implementations are in Python, with a Java/Spring view.
78eab95e1e:
The whole chapter collapses into two sentences.

A model can only do as well as the context it is given, so a large task is solved by deciding how to cut it into contexts: cut it in advance along lines you already know (a fixed pipeline, or one pass per file plus an integration pass) when the shape of the work is predictable, and let the model cut it as it goes (map, prioritise, plan, re-plan from findings) when the shape depends on what it finds.

A session is a stored message history that is replayed to the model, so resuming one means the model believes everything in it, including tool results that stopped being true; resume when the history is still true, fork when you want branches from a shared baseline, tell a resumed agent exactly which files changed, and start fresh with a summary of conclusions when the old tool results cannot be trusted.
9c748b3158:
Everything else follows from those two sentences. Decomposition is a decision about how much goes into each context and who chooses the cut. Session management is a decision about whether what is already in the context is still true.

Both answer the same limitation. The model has no access to the world except through the text in front of it.
6aa6220b38:
The exam guide lists these points. For 1.6 (task decomposition):

  • fixed sequential pipelines (prompt chaining) versus dynamic adaptive decomposition;
  • prompt chaining for predictable multi-aspect reviews;
  • adaptive investigation plans that generate subtasks from intermediate findings;
  • splitting large code reviews into per-file local analysis plus a separate cross-file integration pass;
  • for open-ended tasks, mapping the structure, identifying high-impact areas, and building a prioritised plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered.

For 1.7 (session state, resumption and forking):

  • named session resumption with --resume <session-name>;
  • fork_session for independent branches from a shared analysis baseline;
  • informing a resumed agent about changed files for targeted re-analysis;
  • the judgement that starting a new session with an injected structured summary is often more reliable than resuming with stale tool results.
8ed64e2cd9:
One official sample question lives here (question 12 in the exam guide). A pull request touching 14 files gets shallow, inconsistent feedback when reviewed in a single request. The correct fix is per-file passes followed by an integration pass. The distractors are "Use a model with a larger context window" and "ask Claude to be more thorough". By the end of section 06 you'll be able to say why each distractor fails, in terms of a mechanism rather than a slogan.

The session questions are the other half. They test whether you can tell what the agent believes from what is true.
5227bc758d: Chapter 01 (the agentic loop). Every claim about sessions rests on its first fact: a model call remembers nothing, and the messages array is the only memory. Loop termination, the pairing of tool_use with tool_result, and token growth per turn all come back here. They show up in the cost of resuming and in the repair of an interrupted tool call.
22ba31f513: Chapter 02 (orchestration). Its sections 09 and 13 cover decomposition by delegation to subagents, and fork-based session management from the coordinator's side. This chapter is the other half: how to choose the cut (fixed or adaptive), and what a session is underneath the fork.
65bff558c9: Chapter 13 (batch and multi-pass review). Its multi-pass review has the same per-file plus integration structure as section 06. The Message Batches API adds a way to run the per-file passes at half price when nobody is waiting. Batch can't run the adaptive loop of section 07, because each step needs the previous step's result.
d8a5ebbaa4: Chapter 15 (error propagation and large-codebase context). Its scratchpad files, structured state export and /compact advice are the practical form of two things here: section 15 (many short sessions joined by files) and the handoff in section 14. Its coverage annotations are what the integration pass and the final report need when a per-file pass fails.
deffd455b8: Neither half of this chapter is new. Decomposition is older than computing. Session handling is a problem that web frameworks, batch schedulers and notebook environments have each solved in their own way. Tracing the lineage explains why the guide frames the choice as "fixed or adaptive" and "resume or fresh".
4b056f5719:
The oldest answer to "this is too big to do at once" is divide and conquer. The oldest software form of a fixed decomposition is the pipeline. Doug McIlroy proposed connecting programs like garden hose sections in a 1964 memo, and Unix pipes arrived in 1973. grep | sort | uniq -c is a fixed sequence: each stage does one job, and the shell, not the programs, decides the order.

Enterprise software grew its own versions. Workflow engines and BPEL in the 2000s, Spring Batch steps with restart metadata, the order-orchestration flows inside telecom OSS/BSS stacks: all of them share one property. A person drew the flow before any order arrived. Sagas (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987) added compensation for steps that must be undone. That's why Chapter 01 used the saga orchestrator as its analogy.
d42084d84d:
Fan-out followed by a combine step is the other classic shape. MapReduce (Dean and Ghemawat, 2004) is "process each piece independently, then merge". Per-file review followed by a cross-file integration pass is the same structure, with one language model as the mapper and another as the reducer.

The reducer matters. What you lose by splitting is exactly the information that lives between the pieces, and the reduce step is where you win it back.
4d6629617d:
Language models inherited both shapes within a few years of each other. Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) showed that writing out intermediate steps improves multi-step reasoning. Least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al., 2022) made the decomposition explicit: break the problem into subproblems and solve them in order, feeding earlier answers into later prompts.

In late 2022, libraries such as LangChain made "chains" the default way to build applications. The output of prompt 1 is templated into prompt 2. That is prompt chaining, and the guide uses the term for the fixed pipeline.
2eb740e845:
The adaptive shape arrived in spring 2023 with AutoGPT and BabyAGI. They asked the model to write its own task list, execute items, and add new ones. They demonstrated the idea and its failure modes, in public. Task lists grew without bound. Tasks repeated. Agents lost the original goal. And costs ran away, because nothing outside the model constrained the plan.

The lesson that stuck is the one in section 07. Let the model generate subtasks from findings, but keep the plan as an artefact the harness can see, with budgets and coverage checks enforced in code.
f354613eac:
Anthropic's December 2024 essay "Building effective agents" gave the field its vocabulary. It separates two things. In workflows, code orchestrates the model through predefined paths (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer). In agents, the model directs its own process.

The guide's two families map onto that split. A fixed pipeline is a workflow. Adaptive decomposition is the model directing the plan. And the best production systems, as example 06 shows, put one inside the other.
10a8df2e18:
Two more lineages are worth knowing, because the exam vocabulary ("fixed" versus "adaptive") maps onto them.

DAG schedulers such as Apache Airflow (open-sourced in 2015) define a graph of tasks in code before a run starts. The scheduler walks the graph, retries failed nodes and resumes from the failure. That's a fixed pipeline with restartability, and it's what example 01 builds in thirty lines. Airflow's later "dynamic task mapping" (2.3, 2022) is the telling exception. The number of parallel copies of a task is decided at run time, from an upstream result. That's the per-file fan-out of section 06: the graph shape is fixed, the width is not.

BPMN engines such as Camunda draw the process as a diagram that analysts can read, with compensation handlers for saga-style undo. They also include an "ad-hoc sub-process", whose activities a person chooses at run time. That construct is the closest enterprise ancestor of adaptive decomposition: a bounded set of allowed activities, chosen by the actor, until a completion condition is met.

The model-driven version differs in one way that matters for safety. The person choosing in a BPMN ad-hoc sub-process is accountable and slow. The model is neither. So the harness has to enforce the bounds (budgets, caps, coverage checks).
3e94e5a051:
If you worked on Java web applications in the 2000s, "session" probably means HttpSession. The server keeps state in memory (later in Redis, through Spring Session), keyed by the JSESSIONID cookie. The client carries only the key. REST (Fielding, 2000) pushed the other way: no server-side session, every request self-contained.

A language model API is the extreme case of REST. The Messages API keeps nothing. So a "session" in this chapter is not state on a server. It's a log that your side stores and replays in full on every request.
f5be805e34:
That makes event sourcing and checkpoint/restart the closer analogies. Transcripts are an append-only event log. "The state" is what you get by replaying it into the model. A fork branches the log at an offset, the way a git branch shares history up to a commit.

The hazard of replaying a log is an old one too. A Jupyter notebook kernel keeps in-memory state from cells you ran last week, while the file on disk has changed. The notebook looks consistent until you run a cell that depends on the stale variable. A resumed agent is that kernel.
7a0efd86fe: Coding agents made this concrete in 2025. Claude Code stores every conversation as a local transcript, so you can leave and come back (--continue, --resume, /resume). It added naming so work in progress is findable, and forking for trying two directions. The Agent SDK exposed the same mechanism to programs: a session id on every result, resume to return to it, fork_session to branch from it. Section 09 onward unpacks what those do.
fa055235c5: Decomposition is only worth its coordination cost where a single context performs badly. So it helps to separate what is mechanical from what is empirical. Three effects are in play, and only one of them can be demonstrated without a real model.
c7018da054: Output budget (mechanical). Every response has a max_tokens ceiling, and one response that must cover 14 files spends that ceiling across all of them. Findings for the first files are written in full. Then the budget thins and runs out. The response either ends with stop_reason: "max_tokens" or covers the later files more tersely than the earlier ones. Raising max_tokens moves the cliff but doesn't remove it, because the work still has to be done inside one response.
3f28374eb1: Attention spread (empirical). A long prompt is not read uniformly. Published long-context evaluations report that information at the start and end of a long input is used more reliably than information in the middle. The "lost in the middle" results are the best known: Liu et al., 2023 (later published in Transactions of the ACL in 2024) found accuracy was highest when the relevant passage was at the start or end of the input, and fell when it was in the middle. The same evaluations report that a model asked to do many things over many documents does each one less thoroughly than a model asked to do one thing over one document. How much depends on the model and the task, so the right response is to measure on your own data (Domain 5 returns to this). This effect is why reviews of large inputs come out generic ("consider adding error handling") and miss specifics in the later files.
3353f060a8: Inconsistency (empirical, and visible to users). When one pass reviews 14 files, the standard it applies drifts. A missing null check is a blocker in file 2 and unmentioned in file 11. Separate passes with the same rubric make the standard a property of the prompt, not of the order of the files.
a8bb4f91c4:
A context window of hundreds of thousands of tokens doesn't change this. Fitting the 14 files into the window is the easy half of the problem. That's why "use a model with a larger context window" is tempting, and why it's wrong. The window limits what can go in. The output budget and the spread of attention limit what comes out well.

Example 03 reproduces the output-budget part with a deterministic stand-in: 14 files in one request, a shared budget, and a response cut off after three findings. It says plainly that attention dilution can't be simulated offline, and tells you to measure it (README lab 1).
cfb8021409:
Decomposition also buys things that have nothing to do with attention. Each step can be validated before the next runs. A failed step can be retried without redoing the others. Independent steps can run in parallel. And each step can use the cheapest model that is good enough for it. If you've split a monolithic batch job into restartable stages, or a service into bounded contexts, you already know why.

The price is coordination. Every split creates a boundary, and context must be passed across it explicitly. Anything that lives between the pieces can fall through. The rest of Part 1 is about choosing where to cut, and what to pass across the cut.
efebadfb67: The guide contrasts two ways of cutting a task. The practical question that separates them is short: do I know the steps before I see the input? If yes, you write the steps. If no, the model has to write them, and your job becomes bounding what it can do.
8bf2f7b668:
Between the two sit the patterns that are fixed in shape but data-dependent in size.

  • Parallelization (sectioning, or running the same job per item) is how you review 14 files. The structure is known (one pass per file, then integrate) even though the number of files is not.
  • Routing classifies the input and sends it down one of several fixed paths.
  • Orchestrator-workers lets a coordinator choose the subtasks while the workers are fixed.

Each is a point on the line between "I wrote the steps" and "the model writes the steps". The exam usually asks you to put a described task at the right point on it.
983d72de4c: A prompt chain is ordinary code that calls the model several times. It passes the output of one call into the next, with checks in between. The model never decides the order. Three design rules turn that from a diagram into something that holds up in production.
e3a9df6d97: One narrow job per step. "Extract the fields" and "decide the category" are different jobs with different failure modes. A step that does both fails in ways you can't attribute. A narrow step also gets a short prompt, which is easier to test and to change.
cc01a1b8cb: Structured output across every boundary. Force the result into a tool schema (tool_choice of type tool; Domain 4 covers it). The next step then receives a typed object, not prose to be re-parsed. The schema is the contract between steps, the way a DTO is the contract between services.
67d6f2c59b: A gate in code between steps. After each step, plain code checks what crossed the boundary: types, ranges, formats, referential checks (does this invoice exist?), arithmetic checks. A failed gate retries that step only, with the validation error added to the prompt. After a small number of attempts, it escalates. The chain never continues on data that failed its gate.
08e10c2c3d: Run it, and the first extract attempt is rejected: the model returned the amount as the string "$128.40". The wire traffic for that step is worth reading once. The request forces the tool:
1d56bff44d:
Two things are worth noticing.

First, a schema alone didn't prevent the bad value. Schemas constrain structure, and the model can still produce a value the schema description discouraged. So the gate is not redundant.

Second, the failure is cheap. run_step_with_gate sends the same prompt plus the rejection message. The second answer has claimed_cents: 12840, and the chain continues. Total: four model calls for three steps, and the order of steps never depended on model output.
3b3b2db5d1: The tempting version passes whatever came back straight to the next step. It works in the demo, because the first call returns clean data. Weeks later it fails on the one email where it doesn't.
c11c704fb9: The fix is the one above: validate at each boundary, and retry the step that produced the bad value. The principle reaches beyond models. Put validation where data crosses a trust boundary, not where it is finally used. A step boundary is a trust boundary, because the model produced what's on the other side.
5c580afe63:
Every extra step adds a model call (latency, cost) and a chance of an error that the next step trusts. If each ungated step is right 95% of the time, five steps in a row are right about 77% of the time (0.955). Gates change the arithmetic. A failure caught at a gate becomes a retry instead of a wrong answer.

So the practical guidance is this. Split where a split gives you something: a different model size, an independent check, a place to validate, a parallel branch. Merge steps that have no checkable output between them. A chain of six steps with one gate is worse than a chain of three with three.
56ef47c42d:
This is the guide's canonical decomposition problem, so we'll do it end to end. The setup (companion pr_fixture.py): a pull request titled "rating-service: move prices to cents, add roaming surcharge" touches 14 files of a telecom rating and billing service.

Each file looks acceptable by itself, except for five local defects: a SQL statement built by string concatenation, floating point used for money in two places, an MSISDN written to the log, and an unbounded cache. Three more defects exist only between files:
6fc01b4760:
Read the trace as three separate failures.

The tail of the diff got nothing. That's the shared output budget at work (the companion stand-in spends output per finding in file order, which a real model only approximates).

No cross-file finding appeared. The prompt never asked the model to extract and compare contracts. And a model reading 14 files in one pass is attending to every line at once, not recording what each file promises and expects.

The review was also shallow, in a way the transcript can't show. That part is empirical. In a real run you'd see it as generic comments on the later files.
69f61055b3:
Now the two wrong fixes the exam offers.

A larger context window changes where the 14 files fit. It doesn't change what the response can hold, or how attention is spread across the files. The output budget in the trace above is the same with it.

"Be more thorough" is an instruction to the same single pass. It adds no output budget. It doesn't separate the standards applied to file 2 and file 12. And it doesn't create a step that compares files.

A third tempting fix is to run the same single prompt three times and merge. That multiplies cost without changing any of those three properties.
3f87d6147e:
Two details carry most of the value.

First, the integration pass can only check what pass 1 recorded. So the per-file schema is a design decision. Ask each file pass to record what the file produces (public signatures, events, columns), what it consumes and what unit or type it assumes, what it renamed or removed, and what retry or timeout policy it applies.

Second, the integration pass receives those facts, not the sources. Paste all 14 files back in and you've rebuilt the single-request problem, with one extra step.
9648612cec:
After all 14 return, the harness compacts the contract facts (dropping empty fields, the findings and the source) and sends one integration request. The three cross-file defects surface because the facts line up:

  • RateCard.java produces priceCents in cents, while InvoiceLineBuilder.java consumes it assuming dollars;
  • UsageEvent.java renamed mb, and UsageConsumer.java still reads "mb";
  • BillingGateway.java has 3 attempts around PaymentClient, which has 3 of its own.
e9f2541b13: Same rubric in every file pass. Put severity definitions and reporting rules in the system prompt, identical for all 14 calls. That fixes the inconsistency problem. And because the prefix is identical, it can be served from the prompt cache. Fan out after the first call has written the prefix, and check cache_read_input_tokens in the usage block to confirm the reads happen. Companion 18_cost_model.py puts numbers on it: with a stable prefix, per-file plus integration costs about 1.1 times the single request in input, with the placeholder prices.
b5215d12b8: Bound the parallelism. A worker pool of 4 to 8 is usually enough. The limit is your rate limit, not your CPU. A failed file is retried alone, which is one of the benefits of the split.
2142a69a9a: Let the integration pass look things up. If it suspects a mismatch, it should be able to open the two files involved (a Read tool, or the relevant snippets) instead of receiving all 14 up front. Targeted retrieval keeps the context small and the check precise.
d376532bb2: Merge in code. Deduplicate by file, line and rule, and sort by severity. Keep local and cross-file findings labelled differently, so reviewers know which kind they're looking at. There's no reason to spend a model call on sorting.
afb17c3b1f: Know what remains. The integration pass sees only what the file passes recorded. A cross-file problem that no pass thought to record is invisible. So when you find a defect the schema missed, review the schema.
ceb7bac874:
Some questions can't be cut in advance. "Why did prepaid churn rise in the Southeast in March?" might have one cause or four, in billing or in marketing or in a release. What to look at second depends on what the first look showed. A fixed pipeline here is a guess written in code.

The guide describes the alternative as a sequence:

  1. map the problem space cheaply;
  2. prioritise what the evidence says matters;
  3. plan subtasks for the top items, and execute them;
  4. re-plan when findings change the picture.

The model writes the plan. The harness owns the loop, the budgets and the record.
ad27057a74: Companion 04_adaptive_investigation.py runs this on a small data set where the answer is hidden. Three things are planted in it: a competitor switcher credit in two metros (more port-outs), a point-of-sale release that dropped payment tokens (more non-pay churn), and a red herring (tenure mix). The coordinator never sees the answer. It sees a table of churn rates by dimension, February against March.
1ccf0657dc: From that overview, the coordinator ranks by movement and writes the first plan. Note the priorities. Tenure moved by 0.1 points, so it's kept, but queued last as a cheap check.
3abca281d6: The adaptive loop is small. What makes it safe is that every limit lives in code the model can't talk its way past. The full version is investigation.py, and 05_plan_file_resume.py uses it.
7c770317fe:
Notice the division of authority, because it's the same one as in Chapter 01. The model decides what to investigate next, and when it believes it's finished (it calls final_report, a structured signal). The harness decides how many subtasks and rounds are allowed, which pending item runs next, and what is written to disk.

The budgets are circuit breakers, sized above a normal run. They raise and escalate rather than quietly returning a partial report.
2f430a8e1c:
The adaptive loop has its own characteristic failures, and each has a known countermeasure.

  • Anchoring: the first strong finding captures the plan, and everything after it is a follow-up to it. An independent cause in another branch of the map is never examined. The countermeasure is the coverage check, plus keeping low-evidence checks in the plan (T3 above) instead of discarding them.
  • Plan explosion: every finding spawns two subtasks. The countermeasure is the cap, and a rule that a new subtask must cite the finding that created it (the evidence field).
  • Premature convergence: the coordinator calls final_report because nothing is pending, although the map had branches nobody opened. The coverage check handles this one too.
  • Loss of the goal: after six subtasks, the original question is a distant memory. Put the question in every coordinator call, not only the first.
112a127d0b: Nothing in this chain is badly written. It's the wrong shape. Steps 2 and 3 are fixed, so the investigation ends exactly where the data first looks explainable. On an exam, "the steps depend on what is found" signals adaptive decomposition, and "a pipeline with more steps" is the distractor.
c82ffae55c:
Production systems rarely pick one. The usual structure is a fixed outer pipeline whose shape you can test, with one adaptive step in the middle, boxed in by budgets and a typed output (companion 06_hybrid_pipeline.py):

  • intake and normalisation are code;
  • the investigation is adaptive;
  • a gate checks that the report has a summary, a confidence and open questions;
  • the final letter is one fixed model call.

The adaptive step is the only place where the number of model calls isn't known in advance. It's also the only place with a call budget.
44ba1f47b6: The guide's example of an open-ended task is "add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase". It's a good test of the vocabulary, because each of its words is a trap. The word comprehensive has no end. The word legacy means the structure is unknown. And a fixed pipeline ("for each class, write tests") would spend its effort on whichever classes it listed first. The three moves apply in order.
8d2f4afd73: Map before you commit, and use cheap tools to do it: directory listings, dependency graphs, the build file, and evidence of where the risk is. In Claude Code, that means Glob and Grep, or an exploration subagent that reads widely and returns a short inventory instead of dumping files into your context. Two numbers do most of the prioritising. Both come from tools, not from the model's opinion:
580e580b95:
Read what happened between the first plan and this one. A finding from T2 added a prerequisite (T5, a seam for the static clock) that blocks two other tasks. Another finding made T4 pointless, and the plan records that it was dropped with a reason instead of silently disappearing.

The plan also carries a known coverage gap. So a harness check can refuse to accept "done" while coverage_gaps is non-empty. That's "a prioritised plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered", as an artefact.
7fe1f48565:
Chapter 01 established that a model call remembers nothing. The messages array you send is the only memory. Everything in the second half of this chapter follows from that sentence, plus a persistence layer.

When Claude Code or the Agent SDK says "session", it means a stored copy of that array, plus metadata, under an identifier. There's no server-side object to reconnect to. A session in this chapter is closest to an event log your side keeps and replays.
44c35e2483: The Claude documentation defines it the same way. A session is the conversation history the SDK accumulates while your agent works: your prompt, every tool call, every tool result and every response, written to disk automatically. The docs also state what a session is not. Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem. Hold on to that. The stale-state hazard is the gap between those two things.
33a2857256:
Names are how a team keeps several investigations apart ("auth-refactor", "billing-q3-outage"), so their failure modes matter. If two sessions share a name, claude --resume <name> opens the picker with the name pre-filled instead of choosing one. /resume <name> reports an error.

Say you start or rename a session into a name that another live session on the machine already uses. Claude Code keeps the name on the older session, and gives yours a variant with a two-word suffix, such as auth-refactor-graceful-unicorn.

Example 07 reproduces the ambiguity on the teaching model. After the second session takes the same name, resolution fails until one of them is renamed.
3f373c5237:
By default, Claude Code stores each session as JSON Lines at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl. The <project> part is your absolute working directory, with every non-alphanumeric character replaced by -. So /Users/me/proj becomes -Users-me-proj. Names that would exceed 200 characters are truncated and given a hash.

CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR moves the whole tree. cleanupPeriodDays controls retention: 30 days by default at the time of writing.

Each line is a JSON object for a message, a tool use or a metadata entry. Anthropic documents the entry format as internal and subject to change between versions. That's the reason to use the SDK helpers instead of parsing the files.
304d99ecd9:
Two details change how you use sessions in automation.

First, sessions created by claude -p or the Agent SDK are left out of the session picker and out of claude --continue. You can still resume one by passing its id to --resume (and claude -p --continue includes them).

Second, persistence can be turned off: --no-session-persistence on a print-mode run, persistSession: false in the TypeScript SDK, or the CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY environment variable. A session that was never written can't be resumed.
a635087e12: The companion's mini_sessions.py is a teaching model of this layout, so you can poke at it without a real CLI. It follows the documented outline (one file per session, per-project folder, parent chain), but it is not the real format. Its entries look like the following.
c1127959dc: To read real sessions from code, use the SDK helpers. In Python these are list_sessions() and get_session_messages() (listSessions() and getSessionMessages() in TypeScript), plus get_session_info(), rename_session() and tag_session(). Example 15 runs them offline against a synthetic transcript in a temporary config directory.
3d6053f3b0:
Two more behaviours are easy to miss.

First, a tool call that was still running when the process died does not run again on resume. Claude sees the call marked as cut off before its result was recorded, and is told to check whether it took effect before repeating it. That's the harness doing for you what Chapter 01's exercise asked you to write: repairing an unanswered tool_use so the next request is valid. The companion's Agent.resume does the same, and 17_testing_orchestration.py tests that without it the API would answer with a 400.

Second, the system prompt is built once, on the conversation's first request. It's recorded in the session and reused on later requests until the conversation is compacted. So changing --append-system-prompt between runs doesn't change a resumed conversation's prompt until compaction or a new conversation.
0e2efd921d:
The SDK splits the same operations into three option fields on ClaudeAgentOptions (Python) or Options (TypeScript).

  • Continue picks up the most recent session in the current directory, without an id.
  • A resume takes a specific session id.
  • A fork branches a new session from the original and leaves the original unchanged.

In Python these are named continue_conversation, resume and fork_session. In TypeScript they are continue, resume and forkSession.

The Python names were checked against the installed package: claude-agent-sdk 0.2.164 at the time of writing. That version also has session_id to choose an id, resume_session_at to resume only up to a message, enable_file_checkpointing and session_store. Example 15 asserts they exist, so a version drift fails loudly instead of silently. Check the docs for your version.
4d356c4a12:
Two operational points.

First, resuming is the documented way to recover from a limit. A run that ended with error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd can be resumed with a higher limit, after catching the error that a single-shot query() raises.

Second, session files are local to the machine that wrote them. For CI workers, ephemeral containers or serverless hosts, you have three options:

  • pass a session_store adapter, so transcripts are mirrored to your own backend;
  • restore the .jsonl file into the new host's projects folder before calling resume;
  • don't rely on resume at all: capture the results you need (analysis output, decisions, diffs) as application state, and pass them to a fresh session.

The documentation itself notes that the last option is often more reliable than shipping transcript files around. That's the 1.7 judgement in one sentence.
281e66b4f1:
Because resume replays the history, the first request after a resume costs whatever reading that history costs. Whether the read is cheap or full price depends on the prompt cache. Here are the facts that matter, from the prompt caching documentation at the time of writing (check the docs for current numbers):

  • The cache lifetime is 5 minutes by default, with a 1-hour option.
  • The lifetime is measured from the start of the request that wrote or last read the entry.
  • A cache read costs a fraction of the base input price (0.1 times is the standard figure; some models are lower). A 5-minute write costs 1.25 times, and a 1-hour write 2 times.
  • A hit requires an identical prefix, ordered tools, then system, then messages. A change at one level invalidates the cache from that level onward.
cb037bc872:
This explains a product behaviour you may meet. On Pro and Max plans, you might resume a session that has been inactive for more than about an hour and holds more than about 100,000 tokens. Claude Code restores the conversation and then asks how to continue. The cache has expired, so the next request processes the full history once, whichever option you pick.

  • Resume from summary runs /compact immediately. It replaces the history with a summary, your most recent exchanges and up to five recently read files. Later requests carry the summary instead of the full history.
  • Resume full session as-is keeps every detail, at a per-request cost that scales with the conversation.

That dialog is the cost version of the 1.7 judgement. A smaller, curated context is cheaper per request. Whatever the summary leaves out is no longer available to the model.
992cf3e462: Budget caps and resume. --max-budget-usd checks a client-side estimate. Totals restored from earlier runs, when you use --continue or --resume, don't count toward the cap. So a resumed run gets its own allowance. Check the cost-tracking docs when you build on this.
52a506463b:
A fork creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original's history and diverges from there. The fork gets its own id. The original is unchanged and can still be resumed.

The guide describes the use case as divergent exploration from a shared analysis baseline. Say you spent an hour and a lot of tokens getting an agent to understand the auth module. Now you want to ask "how would JWT work?" and "how would OAuth2 work?". You don't want either answer to contaminate the other, and you don't want to pay for the analysis twice.
8e4a914172:
The exam distinction is between fork_session and its look-alikes.

  • Resuming the same session twice doesn't branch. Both resumed processes append to the same transcript, and the documentation notes that messages from two terminals interleave into one history.
  • A subagent starts with a fresh context, not a copy of yours.
  • Rewind (/rewind) moves one session back to an earlier checkpoint instead of creating a second line.
  • A new session with a summary keeps nothing of the old transcript.

Each answers a different question. The forking question is "I want two futures from this exact past".
73cb1993ad: A fork branches the conversation, not the working tree. If both branches edit auth.py in the same directory, they share a disk. Example 16 runs exactly this. The JWT branch writes its version, the OAuth2 branch writes its own, and then the JWT branch re-reads the file to verify its work.
cff1fc3232:
Neither session did anything wrong. Each acted on a disk that changed under it: the same stale-state problem, in real time instead of across a pause.

The fix is isolation at the layer the fork doesn't cover. Use one git worktree per branch (git worktree add, or claude --worktree <name> for a Claude Code session in its own worktree), or a copied directory. File checkpointing and /rewind are for undoing a session's edits, not for keeping two live branches apart. They also don't track changes made through Bash or by subagents.
6e1a08bb71:
Here's the central hazard of resuming, stated as a rule: the model treats everything in its context as current unless something in the context says otherwise.

A tool_result in a transcript is a snapshot, an observation made at a particular time. Nothing about its position in the history marks it as ageing. When the history is replayed on resume, a file the agent read on Monday looks exactly as authoritative as a file it read a minute ago.
9a2ee7fde2:
If you've built services with JPA, you know this bug under another name: the lost update. Transaction A reads a row. Transaction B changes it. A writes back its modified copy, and B's change vanishes, with no error from the database. The cure there is optimistic locking (a @Version column, an ETag with If-Match): make the write prove it saw the current version.

A resumed agent is transaction A with a very long think time. The transcript is its stale read.
fb410453a7:
Example 10 sets the scene on the teaching model. On Monday, the agent reads rating.properties and reports retry.max=3. On Tuesday, a colleague changes timeout.ms and adds pool.size=20. On Wednesday, you resume and say "set retry.max to 5".

The stand-in model encodes the premise stated at the top of this section: it edits from the last read it has, unless told that read is out of date. It's a model of the failure, not a measurement of any real model. Whether a given model re-reads without being told is something to test on the model you use (README lab 2).
50ea44961a:
The first fix is the one the guide names. When you resume after the code has changed, inform the agent about the specific changes so it can re-read what's affected. Don't leave it to rediscover everything, or worse, tell it nothing at all.

The mechanism is cheap and needs no model. Record a manifest of hashes for the files the session touched. Compare on resume. Then inject a short notice as the first message of the resumed turn (manifest.py, example 11).
a2f313149c:
If the project is in git, the same job is one command. Save git rev-parse HEAD with the session. On resume, run git diff --name-status <saved>, which covers both commits since then and uncommitted edits to tracked files. Add git status --porcelain for untracked files. Example 11 prints both forms.

A good notice has four properties:

  • It names the files, because "something changed" is useless.
  • It says what that means for the context ("earlier reads of these files are out of date").
  • It lists what is still valid, so the agent doesn't re-read everything.
  • It comes first, before the user's next instruction, so the instruction is interpreted in light of it.

That's the targeted re-analysis the guide describes: re-read what changed, re-derive what depended on it, keep the rest.
8729f52259: The notice can't fix derived staleness by itself. Suppose the agent concluded from Monday's read that "the retry policy is only configured here". If the changed file is where a second setting was added, that conclusion is wrong even after the file is re-read, unless the agent is prompted to re-check it. For analysis sessions, it's worth appending a line such as "re-verify any conclusion that depended on these files".
72a2e9fd80: The second fix is the one the guide calls often more reliable: don't resume at all. Start a new session whose first message is a structured summary of conclusions, and let the new session read the files itself. Nothing in it is stale. The only tool results in the new context are ones the new session fetched a moment ago. Run C in the example does that:
1b65bdc9b2:
Both fixes above act on the model's context. The third acts on the tool, and it's the optimistic lock from the JPA analogy. The write tool takes the hash of the version the agent read. If the file on disk differs, it refuses the write and returns an error the model can act on (Run D in the example).

Some harnesses' own edit tools reject a write when the file changed after it was read. Whether yours does, and for which tools (Bash and custom tools usually don't), is worth verifying in the docs rather than assuming.
8e4f3e5830: Defence in depth is the sensible position. The notice keeps the agent's beliefs current. The summary avoids the problem for long gaps. And the locked write turns the remaining silent failures into loud ones.
f77ea081ea: Section 14 builds the summary. Choosing between the options is a judgement, and writing the judgement as rules makes it testable (13_resume_or_fresh.py). The rules below are this chapter's, not an official algorithm, but each one reflects a documented trade-off.
dd0ea115ac:
Resuming carries everything, which is its strength and its weakness. A transcript contains the useful analysis. It also contains the abandoned approaches, file contents that have since changed, verbose command output, and a lot of text the next step doesn't need. A new session with a summary carries only what you choose to put in it.

The guide says this is often more reliable than resuming with stale tool results. It's worth spelling out why, in terms of mechanism.
877a57cf76:
The cost is that a summary is lossy and can be wrong. A wrong summary is a stale tool result with better formatting. Two rules reduce the risk.

Summaries carry conclusions with provenance, not raw output, and they separate what was verified from what was assumed.

And they carry pointers, not contents: "plan.json holds the subtask list" instead of the list pasted in. That way the new session reads the current file.
999070c96c:
A summary compresses by paraphrase, and paraphrase is where precise values go to die. "The failure rate was high" can't be re-checked; "2.4% of autopay attempts on Mar 11" can. Some values are identifiers or thresholds that the next session will type into a query, a ticket or a commit message. A model that rewrites "pos-v2.4.1" as "POS v2" has changed what the query matches.

So the template reserves a section for facts to keep exact: ticket and release identifiers, version numbers, thresholds and limits that were agreed, file paths, table and column names, and any number a decision depended on.

The rules for that section:

  • Copy values character for character from the source of truth. Don't copy them from the previous summary, which compounds drift.
  • Give each value a name.
  • Keep the list short enough to read in ten seconds.
  • Never put prose in it.

Anything that needs explanation belongs under Decisions or Done.
9aea91fc41:
The section also marks the boundary with Verified. A fact in the exact list is something the next session must reuse unchanged. A fact in Verified is something it may rely on without re-deriving. A value can be in both.

In handoff.py this is the optional exact field, rendered as "Facts to keep exact (copy verbatim; do not paraphrase)". Example 12 asserts that the ticket id survives rendering. When the model writes the summary (variant B), validate the exact values against your own records. This is the section it's most likely to get subtly wrong.
32606c78fc:
This looks like a summary and behaves like a stale resume. It pastes a file's contents as fact, and the new session won't re-read what it has just been given. It says "everything looked fine" without evidence. It names no next step. And it has no section telling the new session what to distrust.

The repaired version points at the file. It records the conclusion with its provenance ("retry.max was 3 when last checked on Monday"), and says "read it before editing". Section 13's Run C is the working form of that repair.
f8148f7495: Some tasks last days, or span more work than any context holds. They can't rely on one ever-growing session. The pattern that works is to treat sessions as short-lived workers, and to keep the durable state in files that any session can read. It's the same lesson as saga logs and batch restart tables: the process is disposable, the record is not.
659d585dd0: Example 14 runs it on three small features. The initializer run writes feature_list.json, with every feature "failing", and a progress.md. Every later session is a new one. It reads the record and implements exactly one failing feature. Then the harness (not the model) runs that feature's check before flipping its status to "passing":
47509b5892: The numbers are toy-sized, but the shape is the point: per-session context stays flat, while a single transcript only grows. Several design decisions make the pattern work. Skip any one of them, and that's where it fails.
a2ff51d2dd: Git is the ground truth for files. The record says which commit each status refers to. A resumed session that disagrees with git log trusts git.
9f8a4f86ef: Name the sessions after the work item (billing-q3-outage, feature-surcharge). Then --resume <name> is usable by the person who needs to pick one up, and duplicates are visible.
b253f9892e: Resume deliberately inside a unit. Within one feature, a session interrupted five minutes ago is fine to resume: the cache is warm and nothing has changed. Fresh-per-unit is a default, not a ban.
6743950147:
Last, undo. Claude Code's checkpointing captures file state before each prompt that starts a turn. So /rewind can restore code, conversation or both to an earlier prompt. The SDK exposes file checkpointing as an option.

The documented limits matter here. It tracks edits made through the file-editing tools. It doesn't track changes made by Bash commands (rm, mv), edits made by most subagents, or changes made outside the session. It's session-level recovery, not version control, and it's a different tool from forking.
a3073459ab:
At the time of writing, the Agent SDK is distributed for Python and TypeScript (check the docs for current languages). So a Java/Spring service has two realistic options.

  • It can call the Messages API through the Anthropic Java SDK or plain HTTP, and own the loop. Sessions are then rows in your database.
  • It can drive the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess in print mode, using the documented -p --resume <id> --output-format json interface and storing the session id it returns.

The first gives you control and a schema you design. The second gives you Claude Code's tools and transcripts for free.
7352de31db:
When you own the loop, the operations of this chapter become ordinary persistence code.

  • Resume is a query that loads the stored messages.
  • Fork copies rows up to a cut point into a new conversation. Cut on a turn boundary, never between a tool_use and its tool_result.
  • The stale notice compares a stored manifest with current hashes.

Companion java/ConversationStore.java is that logic in plain Java (compiled by run_all.sh), with the tables you'd create noted in the header:
ec0e7f05fe:
In Spring this is a @Service over JdbcClient or Spring Data, with three tables: conversation(id, name, parent_id, forked_at_seq), message(conversation_id, seq, role, content_json) and file_manifest(conversation_id, path, sha256).

Two cautions from experience with long-lived records. First, store content_json exactly as the API returned it, including thinking blocks with their signatures (Chapter 01), because the API validates them when you replay. Second, add a retention policy. A transcript can contain customer data, so it needs the same retention and access rules as the tickets it came from.
1d251919a4: If you take the CLI route, the interface is stable enough to wrap. Use --output-format json, read the session id from the result, and persist it with your own job id. Don't parse the transcript files themselves. The entry format is internal.
69164e29a4: What these tests deliberately don't check is whether the real model finds the unit-mismatch defect, or re-reads a changed file when told to. Those are evals. Run the same orchestration against the real API on a labelled set, over several runs, and count. The README labs say how. Keeping the two kinds of test apart keeps the fast suite deterministic.
e7329eef77:
The symptoms map to mechanisms. Shallow feedback on later files is a shared output budget and spread attention. Inconsistent severity is a standard that drifts across one long pass. The missed rename is a defect that exists only between files.

C addresses all three: separate passes with a shared rubric, then a pass whose only job is cross-file contracts. A changes what fits in the window, not the output budget or the attention spread (the 14 files already fit). B is an instruction to the same single pass; it adds no budget and no comparison step. D multiplies cost. And by keeping only findings that recur, it tends to discard the rare cross-file ones.

The integration pass receives compact contract facts, not all 14 files again. Otherwise it recreates the original problem.
a219068497:
The session is mostly still true: 38 of 40 files are unchanged. B injects the specific change, so the agent does a targeted re-analysis, which is the 1.7 behaviour. Its instruction to re-check dependent conclusions covers derived staleness.

A relies on a tool-level guard that may not exist for every tool. It also does nothing for the agent's stale reasoning about signatures it never edits. C pays to re-read 38 files that didn't change. D throws away the analysis and relies on your memory of it.

If most files had changed, a fresh session with a summary would win (scenario 5).
db732656bb:
The requirement is independent branches from a shared baseline, and that's what a fork is for. Each fork has its own id and a copy of the history. The original is unchanged, and the analysis is paid for once.

A resumes the same session twice, so both processes append to one transcript and the two explorations interleave. C pays for the analysis twice, and may produce two slightly different baselines. D keeps both designs in one context, where each contaminates the other.

The caveat in B matters in practice: a fork branches the conversation, not the files.
f5a35e8a59:
The structure is unknown, and findings will change the order. A static singleton needs a seam before its callers can be tested. A dead class should be deleted, not tested. That's adaptive decomposition: map, prioritise, plan, re-plan.

A fixes the order and the stopping point before anything is known. C is the single-context failure of section 03, on a larger scale. D is a fixed fan-out. It spends equal effort on a dead class and the payment retry policy, and it has no integration step for the dependencies. B also names the guardrails (persisted plan, subtask cap) that make an adaptive loop safe.
dfec261335:
Most tool results in this transcript describe volatile state (queues, ticket statuses) with a half-life of minutes. And the branch has been rebased. So a large part of the transcript is out of date. Resuming replays it all, at cold-cache price, and the model will believe it.

A does that. B is a limit fix for a different problem. D asks the model to detect staleness it has no signal for; nothing in the context says what changed. C carries the conclusions and drops the stale observations, and the new session fetches current state.

This is the guide's "often more reliable than resuming with stale tool results".
61fd2c44fa:
The failure is an unbounded adaptive loop. The guardrails belong in code the model can't ignore: a persisted plan the harness can read, caps, evidence requirements, deduplication and a coverage check.

A changes sampling, not the structure. C asks the model to police itself, which is the symptom. D discards the property that made the approach useful for an investigation whose steps aren't known in advance.

Note that the caps are safety budgets. The normal end is the model's structured final_report, after the coverage check passes.
8d744dc75e: Use the companion folder ccarf-companion/04-decomposition-sessions/. Everything runs offline. Create a virtualenv, install anthropic (and claude-agent-sdk for example 15), and run bash run_all.sh. All 18 Python examples and both Java classes should print ok.
0d29aadbf5: Run 02_per_file_then_integration.py --mock and 03_single_pass_baseline.py --mock. List which of the eight planted defects each one finds. For each defect, explain which mechanism (output budget, no comparison step, neither) accounts for the difference.
2a7b8aef85: In pr_fixture.py, add a ninth defect that needs a new contract fact. For example: two files that both set a timeout, where the caller's is shorter than the callee's. Extend _per_file to record it and _integration to check it. Which half of the pipeline had to change? And why was the integration pass blind to it before?
e02136cee3: Run 05_plan_file_resume.py --mock. Then open the plan file it writes, and delete one "done" status by hand before the second run. Which subtask reruns? What does that say about trusting a plan file, and what check would you add?
709fc84f85: Optional, with an API key: replace ReviewClient() in 02 and 03 with anthropic.Anthropic(), and write a real system prompt for each pass. Run both on a real 14-file diff with three planted cross-file defects. Repeat five times, and record defects found per run for each approach.
12b7e37a9e:
Done when you can do three things:

  • explain why each of the three exam distractors in scenario 1 fails, in terms of output budget, attention or missing comparison;
  • having watched run A of example 10 lose the colleague's lines, say which of the three fixes you'd choose for a nightly batch job and which for an interactive session;
  • show that your answer to lab step 6 matches the arithmetic in section 11.
